subtype: Approach: root-cause analysis with five whys [Thinking]
passage: Parul, you asked how I came back from failing two courses, so here it is, and I, Mridul, will be honest. My first thought was "I'm just not smart enough." But I made myself ask why, five times. Why did I fail? I missed the internal exams. Why? I was not in class for the first six weeks. Why? My grandfather was in hospital and I was travelling home every weekend and coming back late. Why did I not fix it? I never told any professor. Why? I was scared of sounding like I was making excuses. When I laid it out, it was about missed classes and not asking for help, not about ability. That felt different. Fixable.

qa.q: For how many weeks was Mridul absent from class at the start?
qa.a: Mridul was not in class for the first six weeks.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling at first about the failure?
qa.a: Mridul felt ashamed and doubtful about ability, thinking 'I'm just not smart enough' before asking why.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Mridul use next term to avoid a repeat, and why?
qa.a: Mridul could tell a professor or advisor early when something at home disrupts classes, because the chain shows that silence turned a short absence into a failed course.

qa.q: How might Parul see Mridul's story?
qa.a: Parul asked how Mridul came back and hears a plain account without excuses, so Parul may find it easier to trust that the failure was fixable.

grounding: Shows repeated why-questions leading from a failed result to missed early classes and reluctance to seek help, rather than to lack of ability.

subtype: Approach: root-cause analysis with five whys [Thinking]
passage: I'm Vaibhav, Thomas's roommate, and I was there the night he finally stopped saying "I'm just stupid." He had failed two courses, Signals and Maths III. He sat at his desk with a sheet of paper and wrote "Why did I fail?" at the top. Under it: "Didn't understand the material." Why? "Missed the first four weeks." Why? "I was home in Kottayam. Amma was in hospital." Why didn't you catch up after? He stopped writing for a while. Then: "I was embarrassed to ask the professors. Everyone else seemed ahead." And why didn't you ask anyway? "Because I thought asking meant I wasn't smart enough." He put the pen down and looked at me. "So it wasn't ability. It was four missed weeks and not asking." I don't know exactly what he felt. But he didn't call himself stupid again that semester.

qa.q: Which two courses did Thomas fail?
What might Thomas have felt when he wrote the last answer?
qa.a: Thomas probably felt a mix of relief and sadness, seeing that embarrassment about asking, not lack of ability, was behind the failure.

qa.q: What else could Thomas do next semester?
qa.a: Thomas could meet each professor early, especially after any missed weeks, and join a study group so asking for help becomes normal.

qa.q: How does Vaibhav see the change in Thomas?
qa.a: Vaibhav notices Thomas stops calling himself stupid, without claiming to know exactly what he felt.

grounding: Shows a student who failed two courses asking why repeatedly and tracing it to classes missed during a family illness and to not asking for help, not to ability.

passage:
Results day, June. Pankaj stared at two red Fs, in Thermodynamics and Fluid Mechanics. "I'm just not engineering material," he told Asif on the hostel stairs.
Three days later. Asif sat with him in the empty canteen with a notebook. "Humour me. Why did you fail?" "I didn't understand the second half." "Why?" "I'd missed the first month." "Why?" "Papa's surgery. I was in Jaipur with him." "Why didn't you catch up?" Pankaj was quiet. "I didn't want to go to the professors. I thought they'd think I was making excuses." Asif wrote it down: "Missed month plus not asking. Not ability."
August. On the first day of the new term, Pankaj knocked on the Thermodynamics professor's door with his notebook. "Sir, I failed last term. I missed the first month. Could you tell me where to begin?" The professor pulled up a chair.

qa.q: Why did Pankaj avoid the professors last term?
qa.a: Pankaj felt embarrassed and afraid they would think he was making excuses.

qa.q: What else could Pankaj do alongside meeting the professor?
qa.a: Pankaj could ask about the backlog schedule and join a study group, so catching up isn't done alone.

qa.q: How does Asif help Pankaj see the cause?
qa.a: Asif patiently asks why again and again, helping Pankaj see the failure came from a missed month and not asking, not lack of ability.

grounding: Illustrates a student using repeated whys to trace two failed courses to a month missed for a family illness and to reluctance to ask for help.
